content.title: Bespoke Kitchens in London: Design, Materials, Costs & Installation
content.summary: Plan a bespoke kitchen with clear guidance on layout, materials, project costs and installation. Explore Nura’s services, articles and real project decisions.
content.body:
A bespoke kitchen is developed around a particular home and brief, rather than selected only from a fixed arrangement of cabinets. Layout, storage, surfaces and technical details should work together. Start by defining what the room must do, then agree how the design will be made and installed.

What does bespoke mean for your kitchen?

The useful question is not whether a kitchen looks individual. It is which parts can be designed around your requirements. Ask about cabinet dimensions, internal storage, door construction, finish choices and the way furniture meets the building. Different suppliers use the word bespoke differently; a written specification makes the differences clear.

A room with an uneven wall, a period feature or a difficult access route needs decisions beyond a colour palette. For Nura, kitchens and architectural joinery are considered within the wider home. The relationship between furniture, lighting, appliances and adjacent rooms belongs in the early design conversation.

Explore Nura bespoke kitchen services

Bespoke and fitted kitchens: what should you compare?

Decision What to ask Dimensions Which sizes are fixed, and which can be developed for the room? Materials What are the doors, cabinet interiors, edges and worktops made from? Coordination Who checks appliance dimensions, services, access and site conditions? Delivery Who is responsible for manufacture, transport, fitting and handover?



A fitted kitchen can be a suitable choice when its available sizes and finishes meet the brief. A bespoke approach allows more decisions to be developed for the property. Neither label tells you the complete specification, quality or service scope. Compare drawings, samples and inclusions before comparing totals.

Compare bespoke, made-to-measure and fitted kitchens in detail

Plan the room around everyday use

Describe how you cook, how many people use the room and whether it also serves as a place to work or entertain. Think through a normal day: where groceries arrive, where preparation happens and where clean dishes are stored. These routines help establish practical priorities before the island or door style is chosen.



An island should be assessed alongside circulation, storage, seating, appliance doors and the route into adjoining rooms. Available space and the building itself determine what is workable. Bring measured plans where available and confirm the survey information needed before manufacture.

See the Nura design process

Choose cabinetry and worktops together

View physical samples under the lighting you expect to use. A finish that works in a showroom may feel different beside the floor, wall colour or natural light at home. Review the grain direction, edges, junctions and cleaning requirements alongside the larger material palette.



For cabinetry, compare the complete construction rather than assuming solid wood is always preferable to veneer. For surfaces, compare a named product, finish and fabrication detail. The right combination needs to suit use, appearance and the agreed specification.

Solid wood or veneer: compare cabinetry construction

Choose a kitchen worktop: materials, care and practical checks

Porcelain worktops: benefits, care and considerations

How much does a bespoke kitchen cost?

There is no single Nura price for a complete kitchen. Kitchen and whole-home joinery projects are quoted individually according to the agreed scope, specification and installation requirements.

Share your approximate budget when enquiring. The studio can review what it may cover against your brief, materials and installation requirements. Budget options in the enquiry form describe your budget, rather than a published price for a kitchen.

A useful comparison needs a clear list of inclusions. Ask whether the proposal covers cabinetry, worktops, appliances, design development, delivery and installation. Ask for the applicable VAT treatment and any exclusions to be stated in the quotation. Building alterations and work by other trades should also be identified rather than assumed.

Define the rooms and items included in the commission. Compare material and hardware specifications, not only finish names. Confirm the information and approvals needed before manufacture. Ask which site works, appliances and services sit outside the quote. Confirm programme, payment stages and handover requirements in writing.

Compare the scope, not just the total

Item What to confirm Cabinetry and hardware Which rooms, cabinets, internal fittings and finishes are included? Worktops and appliances Are supply, templating, fabrication and installation included or separately priced? Site work Who handles removal, electrical work, plumbing, decoration and making good? Delivery and access Who checks access, lifting requirements and protection of the property? Commercial details Ask for the VAT treatment, payment stages, exclusions and the process for approving variations.

A smaller cabinetry commission and a whole-room kitchen have different scopes. Compare written proposals with the same inclusions before drawing conclusions from the price.

What happens between design and installation?

Start with a brief and the information available about the property. Develop the layout and material direction, then resolve the technical details and responsibilities needed for the agreed scope. Manufacture and delivery must be coordinated with site readiness and access. The precise stages, approvals and programme should be agreed for your project.

For architects and interior designers, identifying interfaces early helps protect the original design intent. Drawings should make clear where joinery meets lighting, appliances, walls and other finishes. Ask how changes are reviewed so the agreed specification remains understandable to everyone involved.

Working with Nura as an architect or interior designer

Agree stage deliverables before setting dates

Stage Deliverable to agree Dependencies to discuss Brief and survey Confirmed priorities, scope and measured information Access to the property, drawings and appliance requirements Design development Layout, material direction and specification for approval Client decisions and coordination with the design team Technical detailing Approved details, interfaces and manufacturing information Final dimensions, services and product selections Manufacture and delivery Confirmed order, production programme and delivery arrangements Approved specification, supplier availability and site access Installation and handover Installation responsibilities, snagging and care information Site readiness and coordination with other trades

Ask the studio for a project-specific programme and identify who signs off each stage. Changing dimensions, appliances or finishes after approval can affect downstream work. There is no verified standard Nura lead time published here; a numerical estimate should come from the team against the actual brief.

See how an ambitious idea becomes a buildable detail

Nura has published an account of a porcelain island that required a lightweight supporting structure and carefully planned delivery. The value of a case study is the connection between a design ambition and the practical decisions that made it possible.

Three planning lessons from the Amersham Road island are especially useful: establish delivery access before committing to the finished assembly; develop support and fabrication details alongside the surface selection; and coordinate lifting and neighbouring access before installation day. The one-tonne assembly needed a crane delivery strategy. These are lessons from that specific case, not requirements for every porcelain island.

What should you bring to the first conversation?

Property location and the current project stage. Plans, photographs and known site constraints. A description of how you want to use the room. Material references and appliance requirements. An approximate budget, target dates and your design team’s details.

You do not need every decision resolved before contacting the studio. A clear account of what matters most is a useful starting point. The next conversation can establish the proposed scope, what further information is needed and how to develop the brief.

content.title: A One-Tonne Porcelain Kitchen Island: The Amersham Road Story
content.summary: Explore Nura’s Amersham Road porcelain kitchen island: slab selection in Italy, lightweight engineering and the delivery of a one-tonne assembled piece.
content.body:
At Amersham Road in Gerrards Cross, Nura developed a bespoke porcelain-clad kitchen island from an ambitious catalogue reference into a working part of the home. The project combined slab selection in Italy, a lightweight aluminium honeycomb structure, Italian manufacture and a carefully coordinated delivery over two neighbouring properties.

The assembled island weighed approximately one tonne. That figure describes the whole piece, not the load on its hinges or drawer runners. The engineering challenge was to preserve a substantial, sculptural appearance while keeping the moving components manageable.

The project at a glance

Location: Amersham Road, Gerrards Cross. Design and delivery: Nura Interiors. Surfaces: Infinity Surfaces; sole UK distributor: Clay International. Hardware: Blum. Manufacture and assembly: Italy. Delivery: the assembled island was lifted over two neighbouring properties into the rear garden.

View the Amersham Road kitchen project

The brief: a kitchen with real impact

The client arrived with a clear ambition for how the home should feel, but without a finished design brief. The kitchen needed to become the focal point of an older property. Rather than beginning with a predetermined style, the early conversations explored what a strong visual impact would mean for this particular room.

Several showroom sessions brought materials, finishes and proportions into the discussion. During one visit, the client selected a futuristic island image from an Infinity Surfaces catalogue. It was a starting point for the design direction, rather than a complete kitchen solution ready to reproduce.



From a catalogue reference to a design for the home

The reference suggested an island with confidence and visual weight: a piece that could read as an architectural object within the room. Nura developed those qualities around the property, considering how the island would relate to the surrounding cabinetry and the wider interior.

That distinction matters in bespoke work. A reference can reveal what a client responds to, but the final design still needs to suit the home, its proportions and its practical requirements. Here, the island became the starting point for a connected material language across the kitchen.

How to plan a bespoke kitchen around your home

Selecting the porcelain slabs in Italy

Nura travelled to Italy to review and select the actual Infinity porcelain slabs. For a large island, small samples cannot show every relationship that will appear across the finished faces. The batch, direction of the veining and arrangement of adjacent pieces were considered before fabrication.

Bookmatching arranges adjoining patterns to create a mirrored effect. On a faceted piece, the positions of the veins and the meeting of individual panels become part of the design. Working through those relationships with the manufacturing team helped resolve the material composition before cutting began.



Porcelain kitchen worktops: benefits, care and considerations

Engineering the island: appearance, weight and movement

The visual concept called for a substantial, almost monolithic piece. Heavy porcelain applied to conventional doors and drawer fronts, however, would have placed excessive demands on the moving components. The team needed a construction approach that connected the intended appearance with usable cabinetry.

The solution described in the project account was a lightweight aluminium honeycomb structure supporting the porcelain. Reducing the weight of the moving components allowed the substantial surface treatment to be developed around the performance of the Blum hardware. This was a project-specific engineering decision, not a standard specification for every porcelain island.

The approximately one-tonne total includes the assembled island as a whole. It should not be read as the capacity of any individual runner or hinge. Hardware selection needs to follow the actual component weights, configuration and manufacturer’s requirements.

Blum MOVENTO: official runner specifications and load-bearing capacities

Manufacturing and assembly in Italy

Once the design and engineering approach were resolved, the island was manufactured and assembled in Italy. Structure, porcelain, hardware and detailing had to be considered together before the piece arrived in the UK. A change to one element could affect how the others met or moved.

This stage illustrates the coordination behind an apparently seamless finish. Design development and manufacturing cannot be treated as separate conversations when the geometry and construction are unfamiliar. The project required collaboration with the manufacturing team to preserve the intended form while resolving its practical operation.

Nura’s approach to design, detailing and delivery

Delivering the assembled island to Amersham Road

The island needed to arrive largely as a complete piece, and the property did not offer a straightforward route through the front. The delivery approach described by Nura was to lift it over two neighbouring properties, lower it into the rear garden and bring it into the house from the back.

Access therefore formed part of the project, alongside design and manufacture. The photograph below records the delivery of the crated piece. For any similar commission, lifting arrangements, site conditions and responsibilities need to be developed by the relevant delivery and installation professionals for the actual property.



The finished kitchen: a connected material palette

The pale veined island became the visual centre of the kitchen, alongside dark veined cabinetry and warm metallic interiors. The photographs show how the contrasting surfaces, faceted form and illuminated storage contribute to the room as a whole.

The client’s original ambition included adding value to the older home. In Hootan Tayebi’s project account, the unexpected result was personal: the owners enjoyed the finished home enough to reconsider whether they wanted to sell. That is an account of their response to the space, rather than a measured claim about an increase in property value.



What this project shows about bespoke kitchen design

The strongest lesson is the connection between understanding the brief and resolving the details. The client did not need to supply an engineering solution. The design team’s role was to interpret the ambition, develop it for the home and coordinate the material, manufacturing and delivery decisions that followed.

For homeowners, that means discussing how the room should work alongside how it should look. For architects and interior designers, it means involving the joinery partner while challenging junctions, moving components and site interfaces can still be developed.

Working with Nura as an architect or interior designer

Questions about the porcelain island

Where was this kitchen island installed?

The project is at Amersham Road in Gerrards Cross. The Nura project page contains further kitchen photographs and details.

Why was an aluminium honeycomb structure used?

The project account describes a lightweight supporting structure intended to reduce the weight of porcelain-clad moving components while retaining the island’s substantial appearance.

Does the one-tonne figure describe the drawer load?

No. It describes the approximately one-tonne assembled island. Individual hardware capacities and component loads need to be assessed separately.

Can this construction be used for another home?

It is a reference for discussion, not a universal construction detail. A new project needs its own assessment of layout, surfaces, support, hardware, access and installation conditions.

Planning your own kitchen or island

Bring plans, photographs and known access constraints. Explain the visual direction and how you want to use the room. Review actual slab and finish choices before fabrication. Confirm who resolves component weights, support and hardware requirements. Agree the manufacturing, delivery and installation scope for the property.

content.body:
Plan bespoke joinery in London: define storage, materials, hardware and installation responsibilities, then discuss your brief at Nura’s Fulham showroom.

What belongs in a bespoke joinery brief?

Start with the room and the people who use it. A library, media wall, fitted wardrobe or kitchen-adjacent storage needs a clear purpose before the finish is selected. List the items to store, what should remain visible and how frequently things are used. Include dimensions, access constraints and your existing plans. Bespoke joinery can connect these requirements to the architecture; the specification and appointment define what the studio will deliver.

Explore Nura architectural joinery services

Resolve the architecture before the furniture

Look at wall junctions, skirting, ceiling lines, windows and doors. Note uneven surfaces and interfaces with stone, flooring or other cabinetry. Share the design intent with your architect or interior designer so proportions and technical requirements are considered together. A measured survey and approved drawings should establish the information that manufacturing relies on. Do not assume photographs alone provide sufficient dimensions.

Plan storage from the inside out

Measure the things you intend to store: hanging clothing, books, equipment, shoes or collections. Consider reach, door movement and circulation as well as capacity. Keep frequently used items accessible. Discuss which shelves or fittings can be adjusted and which are fixed by the construction or hardware. A generous-looking cabinet can still be awkward if its internal arrangement does not match daily use.

Plan wardrobes and dressing rooms

Choose timber, veneer and painted finishes with purpose

Compare appearance, substrate, edge treatment and maintenance for the specified product. Solid wood and veneer are different construction choices; neither label alone establishes the quality of the complete cabinet. Ask to see samples under the lighting used in the room. Consider how adjoining surfaces age and how marks or damage could be addressed. A finish reference should be accompanied by a technical specification.

Compare solid wood and veneer

Coordinate hardware, lighting and equipment

Hinges, runners and pocket systems have product-specific planning requirements. Discuss cabinet dimensions, load, opening clearances and installation details against the actual manufacturer’s documentation. Media furniture also needs a plan for cables, equipment access and ventilation. Confirm lighting locations and the responsibilities of the electrical contractor before manufacturing details are signed off.

Read Blum’s product planning guidance

Compare joinery quotations on an equal scope

Ask which pieces, finishes, hardware and installation services are included. Identify survey and drawing responsibilities, delivery arrangements, VAT treatment and any exclusions. The studio must confirm what your budget covers against the individual brief. Changes after approval should follow an agreed variation process.

Agree a programme around decisions and site readiness

The programme should connect the brief, survey, design approvals, technical details, manufacture, delivery and installation. Identify the person responsible for each approval and the site conditions needed for fitting. Ask what happens if the room is not ready or a selected component becomes unavailable. No universal number of weeks is promised here: timing belongs to the agreed project programme.

Understand the Nura process

Use completed projects as evidence

Look beyond the overall room photograph. Study junctions, proportions, storage and the relationship to adjacent materials. Westover Road is a useful Nura joinery reference for discussion; its details are not a standard specification for every new commission. Bring examples you like and explain which aspect matters, rather than asking for an exact copy without considering your own room.

The Nura London showroom is at 367 Fulham Palace Road, SW6 6TA. Contact the studio before travelling to arrange a visit. Share your property location, available drawings, rooms involved, approximate budget and intended dates. If a design professional is already appointed, include their role and the decisions made so far. A clear first brief helps establish the information needed for the next stage.

content.title: Bespoke vs Made-to-Measure vs Fitted Kitchens
content.seo_title: Bespoke vs Made-to-Measure vs Fitted Kitchens | Nura
content.seo_description: Compare bespoke, made-to-measure and fitted kitchens by dimensions, design flexibility, scope and installation before choosing.

hero.alt: Kitchen island with seating, pendant lighting and integrated cabinetry
hero.caption: A kitchen layout brings preparation, seating, lighting and storage into one space.

content.body:
Compare bespoke, made-to-measure and fitted kitchens by dimensions, design flexibility, scope and installation. Know which questions to ask before choosing.

Start with the specification, not the label

Kitchen suppliers use these terms in different ways. Treat them as a starting point for questions, not a guarantee of construction quality, price or service. Ask what can actually be changed, which dimensions are fixed and who is responsible for design and installation. A useful comparison considers the room, your priorities and the written scope.

What does fitted kitchen mean?

Fitted describes furniture installed for a particular room. It does not by itself tell you whether the cabinets use standard dimensions or have been individually manufactured. A fitted kitchen may combine stock units, adapted elements and custom details. Ask for the cabinet schedule and the way fillers, awkward corners and service positions will be resolved. Do not assume fitted and bespoke are opposing categories.

What does made-to-measure mean?

Made-to-measure usually indicates that selected dimensions can be adapted to your room, within the supplier’s range or production rules. Clarify which widths, depths and heights can change, and whether internal fittings and door proportions can also change. A made-to-measure solution may suit a constrained space, but the term alone does not confirm unlimited design freedom or a particular method of construction.

What does bespoke mean?

For a bespoke brief, the design should respond to the particular home, functions and intended details. Ask which elements are individually developed and where product or manufacturing constraints still apply. Hardware, appliances and surfaces retain their own technical requirements even in an individually designed kitchen. Bespoke is useful when the actual scope resolves requirements that a fixed arrangement cannot satisfy.

Read the bespoke kitchen planning guide

Compare the same practical questions

For each proposal, ask about dimension changes, material options, internal layouts, junction details, drawings, survey, delivery and fitting. Establish who coordinates appliances, services and worktops. Request evidence from completed projects and inspect relevant samples. A supplier with fewer finish choices may still offer an appropriate solution; more choices do not automatically mean a better design for your room.

Which approach suits an awkward room?

Start with measured information and the problem to solve: an uneven wall, limited circulation, a low ceiling or a particular storage need. Ask each supplier to demonstrate how the design resolves it. A filler panel may be a sensible detail, while an individually made cabinet may offer a more useful arrangement elsewhere. Judge the completed layout and usable space rather than rejecting a method by name.

Compare costs without assuming a fixed hierarchy

Scope, specification, appliances, worktops and installation all affect the quoted total. Do not compare a cabinetry-only price with a complete installation. Confirm VAT treatment, exclusions and the process for variations. Ask the studio for a quotation based on your individual brief and agreed inclusions.

Ask how decisions affect timing

Confirm the programme for your actual specification and site conditions. Ask when drawings must be approved, when dimensions become final and how changes affect production. Standard units may still require coordination and site preparation; custom manufacturing does not remove the need for clear approvals. Obtain the proposed programme in writing rather than inferring a lead time from the category.

Bring the comparison to a showroom conversation

Prepare the room plans, priorities, material references and proposals you are considering. Ask the studio to explain what is included and where your options differ. Nura’s Fulham showroom provides a place to discuss the brief and materials; arrange the visit before travelling. Choose the approach that meets your requirements within a clear, agreed scope.

children.text: Give each supplier the same layout, appliance list and scope to price.
Compare named cabinet, hardware and worktop specifications, not broad material labels.

Start with the same brief and drawing revision

A lower total may cover fewer cabinets, a different worktop or less installation work. Send the same room information and priorities to each supplier. Record the drawing revision, appliance list and finish assumptions used for every proposal so a later design change does not distort the comparison.

An initial estimate can be useful before a detailed survey. Ask whether the price relies on your measurements, an architectural drawing or a completed site survey, and what still needs checking. Note who will confirm final dimensions, service positions and access before manufacture. A drawing attached to a quote is not, by itself, proof that the site has been surveyed.

Compare the specification and materials line by line

For worktops, check whether the named material and thickness apply to the island, perimeter runs and splashback. A material allowance alone does not describe the finished installation.

Match appliance models and internal accessories exactly. A quote that includes integrated bins, lighting and pull-out storage cannot be compared directly with one that lists only cabinetry. Ask for an alternative to be identified clearly if the proposed product is unavailable; do not assume a substitute has the same dimensions or finish.

Separate fixed prices from provisional allowances

Mark each line as included at a fixed price, included as an allowance, excluded or awaiting clarification. An allowance is a placeholder for a defined part of the brief. Ask what it covers, what assumption produced the amount and when the actual cost will be confirmed. Do not treat an allowance as a guaranteed final price.

Record whether the totals include VAT and request a clear breakdown of the amount payable. Compare the same tax presentation across proposals. Ask for the quotation’s validity period and the process for pricing changes after approval. Keep the original scope and approved revisions together so an addition can be traced to a decision.
Request a written description of every provisional item and its basis.
Ask how substitutions, extra work and design changes will be priced.
Confirm that the cost and programme effect of a variation are agreed before the additional work proceeds.
Record payment stages and what design, manufacturing or installation milestone each stage covers.
Check costs outside the kitchen contract

An exclusion is not necessarily a hidden charge, but it still belongs in your project budget. Add a separate column for work paid to other contractors and another for unresolved items. Ask for a written answer where a responsibility is unclear; leaving the cell blank can conceal a gap between suppliers.
Removal of the old kitchen, disconnection of appliances, waste collection and disposal.
Plumbing, electrical work, ventilation changes and coordination with the relevant trades.
Flooring, plaster repairs, decorating and making good around the new installation.
Delivery access, parking arrangements, stairs, lift restrictions and any specialist handling.
Protection of existing finishes, storage if the site is not ready and any return visit assumptions.
Worktop templating, cut-outs, splashbacks and fitting where these are quoted separately.
Client-supplied appliances, sinks or taps, including who checks dimensions and arranges connections.

What must I approve before manufacture, and how are changes recorded?
Which programme dates depend on survey, approvals, material availability or work by others?
What happens at handover, how is snagging recorded, and who is my aftercare contact?

content.summary: Plan a London galley kitchen around circulation, appliance clearances, storage, light and everyday use.
content.seo_title: Planning a Galley Kitchen in London | Nura Interiors
content.seo_description: Explore single and double galley layouts, walkway planning, storage, lighting and ventilation for a narrow London kitchen.
content.author_bio: Nura Interiors designs bespoke kitchens and architectural joinery for considered homes. This guide brings together practical layout questions to discuss against the measured room and project specification.

hero.alt: Westover Road kitchen and interior project by Nura Interiors

children.text: A galley kitchen succeeds when every run of cabinetry earns its place. In a narrow London room, plan the route between sink, hob and fridge before choosing finishes. Then check the space people need to pass, open appliances and prepare food. The drawings should show these everyday movements, not only closed cabinet fronts.

body_nodes.caption: Key takeaways

children.text: Choose a single or double run from measured room width, doors, windows and the way people move through the home.
Use the illustrated 1200 mm central walkway as a planning target, then verify the clear width on the actual drawings.
Place sink, hob and fridge in a practical sequence with usable preparation space between tasks.
Draw oven doors, fridge doors and opposing drawers fully open before approving the cabinet plan.
Use full height storage, layered lighting and a coordinated ventilation strategy to make the room work throughout the day.
Discuss a galley kitchen brief with Nura
Start with the measured room, not a standard layout

Record finished wall-to-wall dimensions, ceiling height, windows, doors, radiators, pipework and the direction in which people enter. Older London homes can have uneven walls or unexpected service routes, so an initial sketch needs a measured survey before cabinetry is ordered. Mark any passage to a garden, utility area or dining room: the kitchen may be a route through the home as well as a place to cook.

List who cooks, whether two people often work together, what must be stored and which appliances are essential. A generous-looking drawing may still feel tight if a tall fridge door blocks the passage or if someone must step around an open dishwasher to reach the sink. Test the plan against a normal breakfast and evening meal, not just a tidy photograph.
Choose a single run or two facing runs

A single-run arrangement puts the main cabinets and appliances on one side. It can preserve a clearer route, daylight from an opposite window and room for a modest dining or utility function. Its main constraint is the length of usable worktop: a sequence of tall units can leave too little landing and preparation space. Put frequently used functions in an order that avoids carrying wet or hot items across the room.

Two facing runs offer more worktop and storage. They also create more opportunities for open doors and drawers to meet in the middle. Decide what belongs on each side by drawing appliance openings and the person standing at each task. Where one run is shorter, the remaining space might accommodate a tall storage unit without closing off a window or a doorway. The better option follows the real brief and the room, rather than a preference for visual symmetry.
Read the 1200 mm walkway as a planning target

The blueprint below illustrates 1200 mm between opposing cabinet fronts. It is a useful starting point for discussing a central walkway, not a universal legal minimum or a guarantee that every appliance can operate at once. Check the finished clear dimension after handles, projecting worktops and any other obstructions are allowed for. Test the resulting passage against the number of users and the route through the room.

body_nodes.alt: Nura galley kitchen blueprint with a 1200 mm illustrated walkway between parallel cabinets, sink, hob, fridge, appliance opening arcs and full height storage elevation
body_nodes.caption: Galley Kitchen Layout Blueprint. The 1200 mm walkway is an illustrative planning target; final clearances and appliance openings must be checked against the measured room and selected products.

children.text: A dimension between closed cabinets does not describe what happens when a door is open. On the detailed plan, mark the depth and swing of each selected oven, fridge and dishwasher, together with the extension of drawers opposite. Allow room for a person to stand at the appliance and for another person to pass if the household needs it. Manufacturer drawings and the final installation specification should settle these checks.
Arrange sink, hob and fridge around real tasks

The familiar kitchen work triangle is a prompt to think about movement, not a rigid geometry for a narrow room. In a galley, sink, hob and fridge may form a compact sequence along one run or alternate across the passage. Consider where groceries land, where food is washed, where preparation happens and where hot pans are set down. Keep the sequence legible and avoid sending someone through an open appliance door to complete a routine task.

Give preparation a usable stretch of surface and check the relationship between water, heat and electrical fittings with the project designer and installers. A sink below a window may feel natural, but the location of drainage and ventilation can change what is practical. Do not assume that moving a service is simple until the site and construction have been assessed.
Make full height storage easy to use

Floor-to-ceiling cabinetry can make a narrow footprint work harder by using height for pantry goods, small appliances and less frequently used items. Put everyday items within comfortable reach. Deep drawers can bring pans and provisions forward without forcing someone to search at the back of a base cabinet. Discuss load ratings, shelf adjustment, door swing and the exact contents of each tall unit before treating its volume as useful storage.

Tall units also affect how light travels down the room. Grouping them at one end can preserve a more open working stretch, although the best position depends on the windows and the appliance plan. Use material samples in the room, with the proposed lighting, to judge whether a continuous cabinet elevation feels calm or too heavy.
Plan daylight and layered lighting together

Many London terraces and flats have daylight concentrated at one end of a narrow room. Keep the window and sightline in the plan from the start. A light-reflecting finish can help distribute available daylight, but it will not replace task lighting where someone prepares food. Show under-cabinet, ceiling and any decorative lighting on the same drawing as the cabinets, then check shadows cast by people and open doors.

Specify how lighting will be switched, dimmed and maintained before manufacture. Cabinet-integrated fittings need cable routes, access and agreement about which trade supplies and installs them. The plan should remain comfortable on a winter evening as well as in the midday photograph.
Coordinate extraction and fresh air

Cooking in a narrow room can make poor extraction particularly noticeable. Discuss the hob, extractor position, duct route, make-up air and available window ventilation with the responsible designer and installer. A recirculating system and an externally ducted system have different constraints; the right choice depends on the property and the approved design. Confirm the selected product performance and installation requirements rather than assuming a visible hood alone solves the problem.

If the kitchen sits within a flat or a protected building, proposed penetrations and changes to ventilation may need further checks. Keep these decisions in the project scope early enough to avoid designing cabinetry around an unverified route.
Use completed work as a conversation starter
The
Westover Road project

shows Nura’s approach to cabinetry and interior detail in a completed home. It is a useful reference for discussing proportions, finishes and junctions; it should not be read as a template or as evidence that the project uses the galley layout shown here. Bring photographs of details you like alongside your measured plan so the studio can assess what belongs in your own room.
For the broader sequence from initial brief to materials, quotation and installation, read the
bespoke kitchen planning guide
. It gives the galley decisions a place within the full kitchen project.
Bring the right information to a consultation

Share room dimensions or existing drawings, photographs of each wall, an appliance wish list and notes about how many people use the kitchen. Mark what must stay, what might move and any known building constraints. The studio can then discuss a single-run or two-run direction, identify what needs surveying and explain the next design step. An enquiry begins that conversation; it does not confirm a booking, final layout, price or programme.

content.title: Plywood vs MFC Kitchen Carcasses: The £40,000 Kitchen Question
content.summary: Compare plywood and MFC kitchen carcasses by board specification, edge protection, hardware and installation, not the showroom finish alone.
content.seo_title: £40,000 Kitchen? Plywood vs MFC Carcasses | Nura
content.seo_description: What is behind the doors of a £40,000 kitchen? Compare plywood and MFC carcasses, moisture details, hardware and the written specification before you buy.
content.author_bio: Joanne H writes for the Nura journal. Explore her professional profile on LinkedIn.

hero.alt: Kitchen cabinet interior with timber cabinetry, integrated oven and visible storage construction

children.text: Plywood is not automatically better than MFC for kitchen carcasses. The right choice depends on board grade, thickness, edge protection, hardware fixing, moisture exposure and installation quality. If you are considering a £40,000 kitchen, ask what the cabinet boxes are made from before deciding whether the quotation represents value. That figure is an illustrative purchase price, not a verified Nura quote, a market average or proof that any particular kitchen uses chipboard. The visible finish tells you very little about what supports the shelves, carries the hinges or surrounds the sink. Compare the actual proposed materials, construction and complete installed scope.

body_nodes.caption: Questions to take to the showroom

children.text: What board and grade are specified for the carcass, shelves, doors and wet-zone panels?
How are cut edges, sink openings and appliance junctions protected?
Which fittings, load ratings, installation work and exclusions appear in the written quote?
What MFC and plywood actually describe

Melamine-faced chipboard, often abbreviated to MFC, combines a particleboard core with a decorative melamine surface. It is widely used in furniture and cabinetry, and its suitability depends on the particular board, thickness, edge treatment, design and installation.

Plywood is built from bonded layers of veneer. The layers can provide a stable and versatile panel, but the word plywood alone does not identify the grade, adhesive, thickness, surface finish or intended application. Neither name tells you everything you need to know.

A well-specified MFC cabinet can be appropriate for indoor use. An unspecified plywood cabinet is not automatically a better one. Ask which product is being used, what thickness is specified, how the edges are finished, where the panel will be exposed to moisture, how the fittings attach and what loads the cabinet will carry.

Ask the supplier to separate the door finish from the carcass specification. A photographed walnut front does not tell you what supports the shelves or how a cut-out beside a sink has been sealed. If a proposal says marine plywood, request the actual panel grade, manufacturer, adhesive classification and finish. Treating the phrase as a promise that a completed cabinet is waterproof would be misleading.
Check the places where moisture can enter

The exposed edges around sinks, pipe penetrations and dishwashers deserve more attention than an interior photograph. Moisture may reach cabinetry through an unsealed cut edge, a leaking connection, steam around a dishwasher, a sink unit with poorly protected joints, repeated cleaning around the plinth or a service hole cut after manufacture.

The material is only one part of the system. Edge protection, joint design, ventilation, plumbing and installation all influence how the finished cabinet performs. Open a sink cabinet, look at the dishwasher junction and ask how the rear service area is accessed.
Manufacturer guidance for
MEDITE MR

illustrates an important distinction: a board intended for intermittently humid interiors is not thereby waterproof. This MDF example is not a test of the MFC or plywood in your quotation. Request documentation for the exact boards offered for your project.
Test hardware and structure against the actual design
Open the proposed tall doors and drawers. Check clearances. Ask how the hinges and runners attach to the selected cabinet panel. Hardware ratings are product-specific. For example,
Blum’s MOVENTO programme
lists different load classes for different runner configurations.

For wide shelves, heavy contents or stone worktops, request the designer’s support details and the manufacturer’s permitted spans and loads. Screw holding, bending and moisture performance depend on the exact panel and test method. A material choice cannot compensate for a design that ignores how the cabinet will be used.
A practical specification checklist
Before comparing two kitchen quotations, ask for the carcass specification in writing. Premium cabinetry is not a material specification.

items.text: The board type and thickness for carcasses, shelves and panels
The surface finish and edge treatment
The adhesive or moisture classification where relevant
Hinge and runner models, including their permitted load ratings
Reinforcement around wide shelves, tall units and heavy worktops
Sink, dishwasher and appliance junction details
Installation, delivery, site preparation and warranty responsibilities

children.text: A plywood carcass may be the right choice for one design and unnecessary for another. MFC may be entirely suitable where the specification, edge protection and installation details are appropriate. The important distinction is between a named board and a complete, accountable system.
Compare the whole quotation, not one board price

A board’s purchase price is only one part of a kitchen quotation. Cabinet design, doors, fittings, worktops, delivery, site preparation, installation, warranty and applicable VAT can change the final scope. A claim that one board costs less at a mill does not prove a saving on a like-for-like installed kitchen.

Ask whether both quotations cover the same number of cabinets, door and drawer finishes, internal fittings, hardware, worktop and splashback scope, delivery, installation, plumbing and electrical coordination, waste removal, site protection, warranty responsibilities and VAT.
Use our
guide to comparing kitchen quotes
for a wider scope checklist, or read the
Fulham showroom guide
for questions to ask while inspecting a display.
Five questions that reveal the real difference
1. What is the exact board specification?

Ask for the manufacturer, product name, thickness and intended use. Plywood can describe very different products. The same is true of MFC. If the specification only gives a general material name, ask for the missing product information.
2. What happens at exposed edges?
Look closely at sink units, dishwasher openings, service voids and cut-outs. Ask how edges are sealed and how the design manages water, steam and repeated cleaning.
3. Which parts are made from something different?
Doors, drawer boxes, shelves, backs and cabinet boxes may use different materials. A timber door does not confirm a timber carcass. Ask for a schedule that identifies each major component.
4. How is the hardware fixed?

Ask how hinges and runners attach to the selected panel and whether the proposed hardware is suitable for the door or drawer size. A product rating is useful only when the product is installed in the way intended by its manufacturer.
5. What is excluded from the price?
A lower headline figure may not include delivery, installation, site preparation, worktop templating, plumbing alterations or VAT. Compare the complete scope, not just the cabinet line.
The drawing is part of the specification

Material decisions make more sense when they are read alongside the design. A tall pantry, a wide drawer bank, a sink cabinet and a cabinet supporting a stone worktop do not place the same demands on the construction. The drawings should show where loads are carried, where services pass through the cabinetry and where access is needed for future maintenance.

Bring the plan, quotation and material schedule together. If one document names the doors but not the cabinet boxes, ask for the missing information. A useful specification should allow another professional to understand what is being supplied without relying on a showroom conversation.
What to take away
The £40,000 figure is only a prompt to look beyond the visible finish. It does not establish what any particular kitchen costs or which board is being used.

items.text: Identify every board used in the kitchen.
Ask how exposed edges and wet areas are protected.
Match hardware to the cabinet construction and design loads.

children.text: The best material choice is the one that is appropriate to the design, clearly specified and properly installed. If you have plans or another quotation, bring them to a conversation with Nura. We can discuss the materials, fittings, site constraints and scope that matter to your project. An enquiry begins that discussion. It does not promise a free comparative estimate, sample delivery, price saving or fixed response time.

content.title: Before You Choose a Kitchen Colour, Test It at Home
content.summary: A simple routine for comparing cabinet samples with your flooring, worktop and everyday lighting before approving a kitchen colour.
content.seo_title: Test Kitchen Colours at Home Before You Decide | Nura
content.seo_description: Compare kitchen colour samples beside your flooring and worktop, in daylight and after dark. A practical routine to help you approve your cabinet finish.

hero.alt: Kitchen palette with light cabinetry and contrasting surfaces

content.body: Before you settle on a kitchen colour, give a physical sample a place in the room itself. View it beside the floor and worktop, in daylight and under the lights you use after dark. The aim is a small, repeatable check of how the finishes work together in your home. Start with the finish you will actually specify Ask for a movable sample of the proposed door finish, rather than choosing from a photograph alone. A painted board can help you explore a colour, but it does not necessarily represent a lacquered door, stained veneer or textured surface. Confirm what the sample represents and what still needs approval. Choose a sample large enough to see its texture and, for timber, the grain. If you are comparing several colours, label the backs so you can return to the same options without relying on memory. Keep the selection manageable: two or three considered choices are easier to assess than a crowded table of swatches. Make a small palette in the actual room Bring the cabinet sample together with the proposed worktop, flooring and wall colour. Place them beside one another, then step back. Look for the relationship you want: a quiet tonal arrangement, a warmer contrast or a distinct change between the cabinetry and surrounding surfaces. Hold the door sample upright where the cabinetry will sit. Keep the worktop sample horizontal. Moving everything onto a table is convenient, but it can hide how the materials will meet when installed. Try more than one position, especially if the room has a bright window at one end and a darker corner at the other. Return in daylight and after dark Look at the same combination in the morning, later in the day and in the evening. Use the room normally rather than searching for one perfect moment. Note whether a colour feels too cool, too warm or simply different from what you expected. There is no need to decide immediately. After dark, switch on the lighting you expect to use together. If the final fittings are not installed, record that limitation and revisit the samples when you can assess a representative light. A photograph can help you remember the arrangement, but use the physical samples for the final comparison. Record the choice before approving it Once a combination feels right, record the product, colour reference, finish and sample identifier with your designer or supplier. For timber, ask how natural variation and grain direction will be represented. Keep the agreed sample available as the design develops. Use a simple colour observation sheet Copy this table into your notes or print it before you compare two or three samples. Add the date, room position and lights used. In each box, describe what you see beside the same flooring and worktop: for example, too cool, warmer than expected or a contrast you like. These are personal observations, not scores or an automatic way to select a winner. Observe Sample A Sample B Sample C Morning daylight Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Later daylight Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Evening lights Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Next step Notes: ___ Notes: ___ Notes: ___ If one combination only feels right at a particular time, revisit it before approval. Mark any missing materials or temporary lighting as unresolved. Keep the physical samples with the notes so another person can repeat the comparison. A documented palette: Ancona The published Ancona project pairs matt black lacquered cabinetry with Palladio Moro terrazzo, ribbed glass and brass handles. The photograph shows why a cabinet colour should be considered with the surfaces and details around it: the cabinetry forms one part of a larger palette.  Use the  Ancona project photographs and specification  to study the finished combination. The published record does not establish how its samples were tested or why the client approved them, so those steps are not presented here as a Nura case history. For your own brief, bring the actual proposed finishes together and use the observation sheet above. For the wider decisions around layout, materials and specification, read the  Nura bespoke kitchen planning guide . For more on cabinet materials, read  Solid Wood or Veneer .
